title: Proposed PFAS Rescission Rule
date_evidence: On May 18, 2026, the EPA announced a proposed rulemaking to correct the Biden Administration's failure to follow the clear requirements of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) ... Last updated on May 20, 2026 (meta-article:published_time: 2026-04-22T12:36:04-04:00 for page creation; the rule announcement itself is dated May 18, 2026 on the page)
key_claim: EPA proposes to rescind the drinking-water regulatory determinations and MCLs for PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA (GenX) and the Hazard Index mixture on procedural grounds, with comments due 20 July 2026; it states the rescission is process-driven and that future re-regulation could be more stringent.
frame_summary: EPA frames the rescission as a lawful-process correction rather than a scientific reassessment, and keeps open the possibility of re-regulating the same substances, possibly more stringently, through a proper sequential process.
verbatim_quote: The EPA’s proposal is solely based on a need to correct this unlawful process.
verbatim_list: On May 18, 2026, the EPA announced a proposed rulemaking to correct the Biden Administration's failure to follow the clear requirements of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA)
While the EPA cannot pre-determine the outcome, it is possible that the result could be more stringent requirements.
notes: Official EPA rulemaking page. The companion proposed rule extends PFOA/PFOS MCL compliance to 2031 via a federal exemption framework (see Ballard Spahr and DLA Piper records for the dated coverage of both rules). title: Reporting PFAS in products (Amara's Law reporting scheme)
date_evidence: Evergreen agency reference page, no publication date; page states 'Initial reports are due by September 15, 2026.' and carries a timeline through Dec. 14, 2026. Accessed 03/08/2026.
key_claim: Minnesota requires every manufacturer of any product containing intentionally added PFAS sold or distributed in the state to report the PFAS, their function and amounts by 15 September 2026, with no product-category or de minimis exemptions, a one-time $800 fee, and a statutory goal of ending all nonessential PFAS use by 2032.
frame_summary: The MPCA argues that because PFAS clean-up is too difficult and expensive to be an effective solution, prevention via mandatory class-wide reporting and phase-out of nonessential uses is the only workable control strategy.
verbatim_quote: a class of fluorinated organic chemicals containing at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom
verbatim_list: The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency (MPCA) extended the initial reporting due date to September 15, 2026.
setting a one-time flat fee of $800 per manufacturer to cover implementation costs
guiding progress toward ending all nonessential PFAS use in Minnesota by 2032

Cleaning up PFAS pollution is too difficult and expensive to be an effective solution, so preventing contamination by phasing out nonessential use of PFAS in products is the best way to protect human health, the environment, and our economy.

title: Support for EU-wide PFAS restriction with targeted derogations: what happens next?
key_claim: ECHA's two scientific committees support an EU-wide restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFAS subject to specific derogations: RAC adopted its final opinion on 2 March 2026, SEAC agreed its draft on 10 March 2026 with a consultation to 25 May 2026, SEAC's final opinion is expected by end-2026, and the restriction covers around 14,000 substances.
frame_summary: CMS argues the committees' opinions make a broad EU PFAS restriction a matter of when rather than whether, so businesses in every sector should assess exposure, alternatives, derogation prospects and supply-chain transparency now.
verbatim_quote: It is the most comprehensive chemical restriction proposed under the EU REACH Regulation, covering around 14,000 synthetic chemicals used across virtually every industrial sector.
verbatim_list: On 26 March 2026, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) announced that its two scientific committees, the Risk Assessment Committee (RAC) and the Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC), support an EU-wide restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), subject to specific derogations.
RAC adopted its final opinion on 2 March 2026.

In the draft, SEAC supported targeted derogations for specific uses where alternatives are not yet available and where cost-benefit analysis justifies this, to ensure the restriction remains proportionate.
SEAC is expected to adopt its final opinion by the end of 2026.
The committees’ opinions reinforce the expectation that a broad EU PFAS restriction is a matter of “when”.

Importantly, RAC recommended that any derogations should be accompanied by risk management measures to minimise emissions, including site-specific PFAS management plans, supply-chain communication, consumer labelling and reporting of PFAS emissions to ECHA.
The UK government published its PFAS Plan on 3 February 2026, which includes an indicative action to align “UK” REACH with the UK's "closest trading partners, especially the EU" by December 2028.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): canonical account of the March 2026 ECHA committee milestone that frames the EU class-restriction track. title: 2026 mid-year PFAS update: How federal and state regulation is shaping compliance and litigation risk
key_claim: State PFAS regimes are shifting from named substances to class proxies (total organic fluorine thresholds, e.g. California tightening textiles from 100 to 50 ppm), reporting regimes are creating marketplace traceability that feeds enforcement and litigation, and key compliance dates stack up from mid-2026 (Connecticut 1 July, Minnesota 15 September) into 2027.
frame_summary: DLA Piper argues that federal and state PFAS regimes now interact to create traceability of PFAS across supply chains, so companies' compliance, testing and disclosure choices directly shape their future enforcement and litigation exposure.
verbatim_quote: some states are beginning to restrict regulated levels of total organic fluorine present in a product as a purported proxy for PFAS regardless of intention
verbatim_list: The reporting requirements are increasing the traceability of PFAS in the marketplace, which may, in turn, influence enforcement priorities and provide a factual basis for future claims.
Tightening of the regulated PFAS threshold for textile articles from 100 to 50 parts per million of total organic fluorine
EPA will accept public comments on both proposed rules for 60 days following publication or until July 20, 2026.
EPA emphasized that this proposed rescission is procedural only and does not reflect any reassessment of the underlying science.

While it remains unclear whether federal requirements will expand beyond perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), many states have already adopted broader approaches, and ongoing research efforts continue to evaluate other members of the PFAS class.
notes: Client alert dated 2 June 2026. The California 100-to-50 ppm item sits in the alert's dated compliance list under January 1, 2027. title: EPA Rolls Back PFAS Regulations, States Fill the Gap
key_claim: While EPA scales back drinking-water standards and extends deadlines to 2031, PFAS obligations keep expanding: CERCLA hazardous-substance designations for PFOA/PFOS stand, TSCA reporting still covers more than 1,460 PFAS, and states accelerate, with Maine and Minnesota heading to near-total product bans by 2032, at least 11 states regulating AFFF, and New Mexico adding a phased ban, reporting and a PFAS product label.
frame_summary: Ballard Spahr argues that despite the administration's deregulatory posture the PFAS compliance perimeter is expanding, because state regimes and retained federal liability hooks (CERCLA, TSCA reporting) more than offset the drinking-water rollbacks.
verbatim_quote: States are accelerating PFAS regulation, with Maine and Minnesota proceeding toward near-total product bans by 2032
verbatim_list: States are accelerating PFAS regulation, with Maine and Minnesota proceeding toward near-total product bans by 2032, at least 11 states now regulating AFFF, and states such as New York developing their own soil remediation standards.

EPA’s Comprehensive PFAS Strategy, announced May 18, 2026, retains the 4 ppt drinking water standards for PFOA and PFOS, proposes rescinding standards for four other PFAS (PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA, and Hazard Index mixtures), and extends compliance deadlines to 2031.

Despite the exemptions, the rule continues to cover more than 1,460 PFAS substances manufactured or imported and PFAS-containing articles manufactured (but not imported) since 2011 under the “known to or reasonably ascertainable” reporting standard.

New Mexico approved regulations implementing the 2025 Per- and Poly-Fluoroalkyl Substances Protection Act, which include (1) a phased ban on the sale and distribution of PFAS-containing products, (2) reporting requirements for PFAS-containing products, and (3) a unique PFAS labeling requirement requiring manufacturers to label PFAS-containing products with the image of a Erlenmeyer flask and “PFAS.”

The retention of 4 ppt drinking water standards for PFOA and PFOS, combined with the unchanged Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) hazardous substance designations, means that liability exposure remains significant for PFOA and PFOS.
The PFAS regulatory landscape continues to expand despite the current administration’s deregulatory posture on other environmental fronts.
notes: Legal alert dated 3 June 2026 summarising two months of EPA PFAS actions and state activity. title: CNA insurers ask court to end PFAS coverage for textile company
key_claim: On 24 July 2026 four CNA insurers filed for a declaratory judgment that they owe no duty to defend or indemnify Standard Textile Carolina in a PFAS suit, invoking an absolute pollution exclusion; the dispute illustrates insurers' push to remove PFAS from standard commercial liability cover.
frame_summary: The trade press frames the filing as part of a wider pattern in which carriers use pollution exclusions and restrictive endorsement conditions to shut PFAS out of general liability coverage, leaving policyholders to carry class-wide chemical liability themselves.
verbatim_quote: no duty to defend or indemnify Standard Textile Carolina, Inc. in a separate South Carolina lawsuit
verbatim_list: The insurers say the primary commercial general liability policies contain an “absolute pollution exclusion” that they contend bars coverage for this kind of claim.

On July 24, 2026, National Fire Insurance Company of Hartford, Valley Forge Insurance Company, Continental Casualty Company and The Continental Insurance Company - together the "CNA Insurers" - filed a declaratory-judgment complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio.
notes: News item dated 27 July 2026 on the 24 July 2026 filing in the Southern District of Ohio, part of MDL No. 2873 fallout. title: Proposed PFOA and PFOS Compliance Extension Rule
date_evidence: On May 18, 2026, the EPA announced a proposed rule to uphold the federal drinking water Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) ... Last updated on May 18, 2026 (meta-article:modified_time: 2026-05-18)
key_claim: EPA proposes to keep the 4.0 ppt PFOA and PFOS drinking-water limits but let systems apply for a two-year federal exemption, moving compliance from April 2029 to April 2031, with interim mitigation required at or above 12 ppt.
frame_summary: EPA frames the extension as upholding the PFOA/PFOS standards while making implementation practical, arguing that more time avoids unproductive violations and lets treatment costs fall rather than weakening protection.
verbatim_quote: two additional years - to 2031 - to comply with the enforceable limits
verbatim_list: The proposed mechanism does not change the PFOA and PFOS MCLs established in the 2024 PFAS NPDWR which remain 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) each.

Under this proposal, drinking water systems with a PFOA or PFOS sample result at or above 12 ppt would be required to implement short-term mitigation actions to reduce exposure to their consumers during the exemption period.
notes: Companion rule to the rescission proposal, same 18 May 2026 announcement; Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2025-1742. Confirms the PFOA/PFOS MCLs themselves are retained.
